dok_rationale: Part (c) weighs a striking pattern against simulated evidence, then coordinates a fair-coin model, an at-least-as-extreme statistic, repeated trials, and a result that would challenge the model.
stem: Suppose a coin advertised as fair is flipped 10 times and gives HHHHHHTTTT. To investigate what chance alone could produce, a class simulates 100 sets of 10 independent fair-coin flips. For each set, the class records the longest run of matching outcomes; the dotplot shows the results.\par\smallskip \textbf{Claim A:} ``The coin is rigged---six heads in a row cannot be chance.''\par \textbf{Claim B:} ``Streaks like this can happen by chance; simulation can tell us how unusual this one is.''
first_take: Which claim seems better supported right now? Cite one detail from the sequence or dotplot.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: State the longest run in the observed sequence and the most common longest-run value among the simulated sets.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Use the dotplot to estimate the probability that 10 fair-coin flips have a longest run at least as long as the observed run. Interpret the estimate in context.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Which claim is better supported by this evidence? Cite the simulation result that settles your choice. Then describe a larger simulation that would more precisely settle the disagreement: state what one trial is, what to record and count, how many trials to use, and what result would make you doubt that the coin is fair.

answers.a: The observed sequence has a longest run of 6, the six consecutive heads. In the simulated sets, 3 is the most common longest-run value, appearing 32 times.
answers.b: Seven of the 100 simulated sets have a longest run of at least 6, so the estimate is $7/100=0.07$. In context, about 7 percent of sets of 10 independent flips from a fair coin produced a run at least as long as the observed run in this simulation.
answers.c: Claim B is better supported. The fair-coin simulation produced a run of 6 in 7 of 100 trials, so a streak this long is possible by chance; 100 trials give only a rough estimate and do not prove the coin fair. For a stronger simulation, use independent equally likely H/T outcomes. One trial is 10 flips; record the longest run of either outcome and mark the trial a success when that run is at least 6. Repeat at least 10,000 trials and compute the successful-trial proportion. A stable proportion extremely close to zero---for example, below 1 percent---would make the observed run very unusual under the fair-coin model and provide reason to doubt fairness. A proportion near the displayed 7 percent would not.

expectedElements.description: Chooses Claim B and cites that 7 of 100 fair-coin trials produced a longest run of at least 6
Defines one trial as 10 independent equally likely fair-coin flips
Records the longest run and counts trials whose longest run is at least 6
Uses many trials and states that a stable, extremely small successful-trial proportion would count against fairness

scoringGuide.E: Chooses Claim B with the 7-of-100 evidence, gives a complete matched simulation with many trials, and identifies a very small stable proportion as evidence against fairness without claiming the current result proves fairness.
scoringGuide.P: Makes the supported claim choice and gives most of the simulation, but omits the at-least-6 event, a large repetition count, or a clear result that would challenge fairness.
scoringGuide.I: Says the streak cannot occur by chance, simulates a different process, counts total heads instead of longest runs without justification, or gives no evidence-based decision.

commonMistakes: Treating a run of six as impossible because each individual sequence is unlikely
Using six flips rather than reproducing all 10 flips in one trial
Counting only runs of exactly 6 and discarding longer runs
Claiming that 7 percent proves the coin is fair
